title: Before Funeral Homes, Burying Your Own Family Was Your Job
fullText: Imagine walking into your dining room and seeing your grandmother's body laid out on the table, not in a casket, not at a funeral home, on the same table where your family ate dinner the night before. Her jaw is tied shut with a strip of cloth. Cotton is packed into her nostrils. Your mother is washing her arms with a rag dipped in cool water. And nobody in the room thinks any of this is strange. For thousands of years, across nearly every culture on Earth, that scene was just called Tuesday. Then, in the span of a single generation in America, all of it vanished. Strangers in black suits showed up, took the body, and charged your family a small fortune to do what your own hands had done for free since the beginning of recorded history. The event that made all of it possible wasn't a medical breakthrough or a cultural awakening. It was a war. But first, you need to see what the world looked like before any of this changed. 1850, rural Pennsylvania. A farmer named IAS wakes up before dawn the way he always does. By the time the sun clears the treeine, his father is dead. Hart gave out sometime in the night. His wife starts heating water on the stove. His mother finds a clean shirt and trousers. Together, the two women wash the body from head to foot. They stop up the nose and mouth with rags. They press coins over the eyelids to keep them shut. They lay him on a wide board propped between two chairs, what people in that era called a cooling board, and they drape a sheet over him while the body stiffens. This was not some backwards tradition practiced by people who didn't know any better. This was the standard. Across America, across Europe, across most of the inhabited world, families handled their own dead the same way they handled their own births. You did it at home because there was literally nowhere else to do it. And you did it yourself because the idea of handing your father's body to a stranger would have seemed almost offensive. The center of all of this was the parlor. Every American home that could afford one had a parlor. A formal room near the front of the house reserved for important occasions. Weddings happened there. Courtships happened there. And when someone died, the body was laid out in the parlor for neighbors and relatives to come pay their respects. The wake lasted 1 to 3 days depending on the season. In summer, you moved fast. Decomposition in the July heat meant a body could become unbearable within 24 hours. Families packed ice around the corpse when they could get it, or draped cloth soaked in vinegar over the face. In winter, you had more time, but the ground was frozen solid, which meant the body might sit in an outbuilding for weeks until the earth thawed enough to dig. Women ran this entire operation. The same women who delivered babies in the community were usually the ones who prepared the dead. They knew how to position the limbs before rigor set in. They knew which herbs mask the smell and which prayers to say over the washing. Children were present for all of it. A six-year-old in 1850 would watch their grandmother's body being washed, would sit in the parlor with the corpse during the wake, would walk behind the homemade wooden coffin to the burial site on the family's own property. Death was not hidden. It was not something that happened behind closed doors in a building you'd never been inside. It was in the house, in the room, and it was part of living that no one thought to separate from the rest of life. and the part that's hardest to believe from where we sit now. Nobody was traumatized by the process itself. Grief was real and devastating, the same as it is today. But the act of caring for the body, of washing your own mother or father or child, was considered a final act of love. You didn't hand that off to someone else the same way you wouldn't hand off the feeding of your infant to a stranger if you could help it. The clock was already ticking on all of this. Within a few decades, an entire industry would rise up and convince millions of Americans that what their grandmothers had done with bare hands and warm water was primitive, unsanitary, and dangerous. In April of 1861, the first shots of the American Civil War were fired at Fort Sumpter in Charleston, South Carolina. Within months, young men from every state in the Union and the Confederacy were dying in numbers that nobody had prepared for. By the time the war ended four years later, roughly 620,000 soldiers were dead. More Americans died in the Civil War than in World War I, World War II, Korea, and Vietnam combined. The old system had worked fine up to this point. Someone died, the family handled it. But the Civil War broke that system in a way nobody saw coming. Because for the first time in American history, massive numbers of people were dying. hundreds of miles from home. Picture this. A farmer's son from Vermont dies at the Battle of Antitum in Maryland. His family [music] wants the body back. They want to wash him, dress him, bury him in the family plot behind the barn the way their people have always done. But it is September of 1862. The body is lying in a field in the late summer heat. By the time anyone could transport it by wagon and rail back to Vermont, there would be nothing left to bury. Families were desperate, wealthy families especially. They were writing letters to anyone who would listen, begging for their sons to be sent home. And into that desperation walked a man named Doctor Thomas Holmes, a New York physician who had been experimenting with chemical preservation techniques borrowed from French anatomists. Holmes figured out that injecting arsenic based chemicals into the arterial system of a corpse could slow decomposition for weeks, sometimes months. He set up shop near the battlefields and started offering his services to grieving families for a fee. This part of the story rarely gets mentioned, but Holmes was not working for the army. He was not part of any official program. He was a private entrepreneur who saw an opportunity in mass death and took it. He personally embarmed over 4,000 soldiers during the war, charging families around $100 per body, which in 1863 was roughly $3,000 in today's money. Other imbalmer followed. They set up tents near the battlefields, advertised in newspapers, and competed for business. The whole operation was completely unregulated. Anyone with a syringe and a bottle of chemicals could call themselves an imbalmer and start charging families. If you're wondering how that was even possible, so was the army. Union commanders eventually had to issue orders restricting where inbalmers could set up because the tents were interfering with military operations. But the detail that everyone missed at the time was what this was really doing to American culture. Imbaling was not just preserving bodies. It was changing what Americans expected a dead person to look like. Before the war, you saw death as it actually was. Discoloration, bloating, the smell. You saw your father's body change over 2 days in the parlor, and you understood on a visceral level that this person was gone. Embalming erased all of that. A properly imbalmed body looked peaceful. It looked asleep. It looked, for lack of a better word, acceptable in a way that an unimbalmed body after 48 hours simply did not. That shift in expectation was about to become permanent. Because on April 15th, 1865, President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated at Ford's Theater in Washington. His body was imbalmed, placed in an elaborate open casket, and loaded onto a funeral train that traveled 1,700 m over 13 days, stopping in cities across the eastern United States so the public could view the body. Millions of Americans stood in line to see Lincoln's preserved corpse. In Philadelphia alone, over 300,000 people filed past the open casket in a single day. They saw a president who had been dead for nearly 2 weeks and still looked like he was sleeping. That funeral train did more to normalize professional death care than any advertisement ever could. Ordinary Americans saw what preservation could do. And suddenly the version they had at home, the cooling board, the coins on the eyes, the vinegar soaked cloth over a face that was already starting to change looked crude. It looked poor. It looked like something people did because they had no other choice. The war ended. The soldiers who survived came home. But the imbalmer did not go back to being regular physicians or chemists. They had discovered something far more reliable than battlefield medicine. They had discovered that grief was a market. That families in their worst moments would pay almost anything to make death look less like death. and that once you convince someone that professionals should handle the dead, it was nearly impossible to convince them to go back to doing it themselves. Within a decade of the war's end, imbalming parlors were opening in cities across the country. The men who ran them needed a new title, something more respectable than embarmmer, which still carried the stench of battlefield tents and arsenic. They started calling themselves undertakers. When that word started to feel too associated with death, they rebranded again. They became funeral directors. The first thing they needed was a building. During the war, imbalming happened in tents, in barns, on kitchen tables. That was fine for a crisis, but it wasn't a business model. So, in the 1870s and 1880s, dedicated funeral parlors started appearing in American cities. These were commercial spaces designed specifically for the preparation and display of the dead. For the first time in history, the body left the family home and went somewhere else. This changed more than logistics. It changed language. When the parlor was where you laid out your dead, every home had one. Once the funeral industry built its own parlor, the words started to feel morbid. Families didn't want a room in their house that shared a name with the place where strangers handled corpses. By the early 1900s, architects and real estate developers started calling that front room something different. They called it the living room. Every time you say living room, you are using a word that exists because the funeral industry made parlor sound like death. And what happened next wasn't just an industry growing. It was an industry actively convincing Americans that they were incapable of doing something their families had done for centuries. Funeral directors launched a quiet but effective campaign through medical journals, women's magazines, and local newspapers. The message was consistent. Handling the dead at home was unsanitary. It exposed your family to disease. It was psychologically damaging to children. The implication was clear. A family that handled their own dead was either too poor or too ignorant to do the right thing. None of this was based on real public health science. By the way, a dead body that hasn't been autopsied or killed by a handful of specific diseases poses almost no infection risk to the people handling it. But the funeral industry understood something important. You don't need facts when you have fear. And nothing generates fear quite like telling a grieving mother that her dead child's body might make her other children sick. Then came the caskets. For most of American history, the dead were buried in simple wooden coffins, often built by a family member or the local carpenter. Hexagonal, narrow at the head and feet, wider at the shoulders. Functional, cheap, easy to build in an afternoon. The funeral industry replaced these with rectangular caskets made of hardwood, then metal, then sealed steel with gaskets and velvet linings and decorative handles. Each upgrade came with a price increase and a sales pitch. The fancier the casket, the more you loved the person inside it. In plain terms, an industry took something a family could build for the cost of lumber and nails and turned it into a product that by the midentth century cost more than the monthly salary of a workingclass American. If you're finding this interesting, hit subscribe. I cover stories like this every week. By 1960, the American funeral industry had become a multi-billion dollar business. Embalming was treated as mandatory even though no state actually required it by law for a standard burial. Families were purchasing sealed caskets, concrete burial vaults, elaborate floral arrangements, printed programs, limousine services, and preparation fees that covered everything from washing the body to applying cosmetics. The industry thought it was untouchable. But a journalist in California was about to blow the whole thing open. Jessica Mittford was a British-born investigative journalist. In 1963, she released The American Way of Death, a detailed examination of how the funeral industry operated. She documented the upselling tactics used on grieving families. She showed how funeral directors would steer customers toward the most expensive options by placing cheap caskets in poorly lit rooms next to luxurious models. She revealed that many of the services families were paying for, including imbalming, were not legally required, but were presented as though they were. The book sold out its first printing almost immediately and stayed on bestseller lists for months. The funeral industry attacked Mitford personally, called her an outsider who didn't understand American death customs, and lobbied against proposed regulations. Instead of reforming, funeral directors doubled down. They pushed state legislatures to pass licensing laws that made it illegal in many states for a family to bury their own dead without a licensed funeral director present. They lobbyed for regulations requiring imbalming for any body that would be publicly viewed. They created a system where the only legal path from death to burial ran directly through their businesses. By the 1980s, the average American funeral cost more than $4,000. By 2000, it was over 6,000. By 2020, the national median had crossed $9,000. And that number didn't include the cemetery plot, the headstone, or the burial vault that most cemeteries required. A family in 1850 buried their dead for the cost of a pine coffin, and an afternoon of labor. A family in 2020 was expected to spend more than some people's annual savings. for the same result. A body in the ground. But the cost of handing death over to strangers was never just financial. The real price was psychological. And it took decades for anyone to start measuring it. Think about a child in 1850 rural Ohio who watches their grandmother die in the back bedroom. They sit with the body while their mother washes it. They touch the cold skin. They help carry the wooden coffin to the family burial plot and watch their father shovel dirt into the hole. That child understood death in their hands, in their muscles, in the smell of soil and wood and cold skin. Now, compare that to a child a century later in suburban Ohio who's told that grandma went to sleep and gets taken to a place called a funeral home where strangers made her look nice. The child sees a version of their grandmother lying in a silklinined box wearing makeup, looking like a wax figure of someone they used to know. They're told not to touch her. They sit in a room full of folding chairs and organ music. And then everyone drives to a cemetery where a man in a suit says some words and the box goes into the ground. That child never saw the dirt, never carried anything, never touched death at all. What that shift created across an entire culture was a society that became genuinely afraid of dead bodies. Americans went from being people who washed their own parents' corpses to people who couldn't be in the same room as an open casket without feeling nauseated. That didn't happen by accident. It happened because an industry removed the public from the process for so long that the process itself became alien. Grief researchers started noticing something in the late 20th century. Families who had physical involvement in caring for their dead, washing the body, dressing it, sitting with it overnight, reported different grief outcomes than families who handed everything to a funeral home. The families who touched their dead described a sense of completion, a feeling that they had done the last thing they could do for the person they loved. The families who outsourced everything more often described a sense of disconnection as though the death hadn't fully registered because they never confronted it physically. Cross-cultural evidence supports this everywhere. In Jewish tradition, the Chevra Kadisha, the burial society, washes and dresses the body by hand as a sacred duty. In Muslim communities around the world, family members perform the goosel, a ritual washing that is considered one of the final acts of respect. In rural communities across Latin America, subsaharan Africa, and parts of Southeast Asia, home burial never disappeared at all. These cultures did not develop higher rates of trauma around death. Research suggests the opposite. Societies that maintain physical contact with the dead tend to have lower rates of complicated grief and prolonged mourning disorders. The American model of sanitized, outsourced, professionally managed death is the historical outlier. On top of the cultural cost, modern American burial practices pump an estimated 800,000 gallons of imbalming fluid into the ground every year. Most of it formaldahhide, a known carcinogen. Hardwood and metal caskets consume millions of board feet of lumber and tons of steel annually. Concrete burial vaults add another layer of material that will sit underground for centuries without decomposing. All of this to accomplish something that a cotton shroud and a 3-ft hole in the earth accomplished perfectly well for thousands of years. But something has been shifting quietly without much fanfare. A growing number of American families have started saying no. The modern home funeral movement began picking up momentum in the early 2000s. Driven by families who looked at the cost, the chemicals, the impersonal nature of the modern funeral and decided to do it themselves. Organizations like the National Home Funeral Alliance started providing guides, training, and legal resources for families who wanted to care for their own dead the way their greatgrandparents once did. And this is the part that catches people offguard. In the majority of American states, home funerals are completely legal. Only a handful of states require a licensed funeral director to be involved in the burial process. In most of the country, you can legally keep a body at home, wash and dress it yourself, place it in a shroud or a simple wooden box, and bury it on private land as long as you file the proper paperwork and follow local zoning regulations. The funeral industry spent over a century building the impression that you needed them. Legally, in most places, you don't. The green burial movement has grown alongside this. Conservation cemeteries across the United States now offer burial without imbalming, without concrete vaults, without sealed caskets. Bodies wrapped in cotton or linen shrouds go directly into the earth at a depth that allows natural decomposition to do what it has always done. Some of these cemeteries double as nature preserves where each burial contributes to the restoration of native grasslands and forests. You die, you go into the ground, and a wild flower meadow grows where your body used to be. Death duelers have emerged as a modern echo of the women who once handled death care in every American community. These are trained practitioners who guide families through the process of caring for their dead at home. They help with the legal paperwork. They teach families how to wash and dress the body. They provide emotional support during the wake. And they help coordinate home burial logistics. They are not funeral directors. They are not selling caskets or imbalming services. They are helping families remember how to do something that was taken from them so gradually they didn't realize it was gone. The families who choose this path describe the experience in remarkably similar terms. They talk about the weight of the body, the temperature of the skin, the strange intimacy of buttoning a shirt over a chest that is no longer breathing. They talk about how different it felt from standing in a funeral home, looking at a body that had been made to look like something it wasn't. They talk about feeling for the first time like they had actually said goodbye. This story is not really about funeral homes. It is not really about imbalming or caskets or licensing laws. Those are the details, but they are not the point. Somewhere along the way, Western culture decided that death was a problem to be managed by professionals rather than a reality to be faced by families. We outsourced the most human experience there is. And in doing so, we lost the ability to sit with it. A growing number of people are deciding they want that ability back. Not because it is easy, not because it is cheap, because it is theirs. Anyway, that's it for this one. If you want to see how another everyday industry was built on convincing you that you couldn't do things yourself, check out that video next. And if you made it this far, subscribe.

Những gia đình thuê ngoài mọi thứ thường mô tả cảm giác mất kết nối như thể cái chết vẫn chưa được ghi lại đầy đủ vì họ chưa bao giờ đối mặt với nó về mặt thể chất. Bằng chứng đa văn hóa ủng hộ điều này ở khắp mọi nơi. Theo truyền thống của người Do Thái, Chevra Kadisha, tổ chức mai táng, tắm rửa và mặc quần áo cho thi thể bằng tay như một nghĩa vụ thiêng liêng. Trong các cộng đồng Hồi giáo trên khắp thế giới, các thành viên trong gia đình thực hiện nghi lễ tắm rửa đó được coi là một trong những hành động tôn trọng cuối cùng. Tại các cộng đồng nông thôn trên khắp Châu Mỹ Latinh, Châu Phi cận Sahara và một số vùng ở Đông Nam Á, nhà việc chôn cất không bao giờ biến mất chút nào. Những nền văn hóa này không phát triển tỷ lệ chấn thương cao hơn xung quanh cái chết. Nghiên cứu cho thấy điều ngược lại. Những xã hội duy trì tiếp xúc thân thể với người chết có xu hướng có tỷ lệ thấp hơn đau buồn phức tạp và rối loạn tang chế kéo dài. Mô hình cái chết được vệ sinh, thuê ngoài, quản lý chuyên nghiệp của Mỹ là một ngoại lệ trong lịch sử. Ngoài chi phí văn hóa, các hoạt động chôn cất hiện đại của Mỹ còn tiêu tốn khoảng 800.000 hàng gallon chất lỏng ngâm vào lòng đất mỗi năm. Hầu hết trong số đó là formaldahhide, một chất gây ung thư được biết đến. Những chiếc quan tài bằng gỗ cứng và kim loại tiêu thụ hàng triệu feet ván gỗ và hàng tấn thép hàng năm. Hầm chôn cất bằng bê tông thêm một lớp vật liệu nữa sẽ nằm dưới lòng đất trong nhiều thế kỷ mà không bị phân hủy. Tất cả những điều này là để đạt được điều gì đó mà một tấm vải liệm bằng vải bông và một cái lỗ dài 3 ft trên trái đất đã được thực hiện một cách hoàn hảo trong hàng ngàn năm. Nhưng có điều gì đó đang diễn ra một cách lặng lẽ mà không hề phô trương. Ngày càng nhiều gia đình Mỹ bắt đầu nói không. Phong trào tang lễ tại nhà hiện đại bắt đầu phát triển vào đầu những năm 2000. Được thúc đẩy bởi các gia đình đã xem xét chi phí, hóa chất, tính chất khách quan của đám tang hiện đại và quyết định tự mình làm việc đó. Các tổ chức như Liên minh Tang lễ Tại nhà Quốc gia bắt đầu cung cấp hướng dẫn, đào tạo và nguồn lực pháp lý dành cho những gia đình muốn chăm sóc người thân đã khuất theo cách của ông bà họ đã từng làm vậy. Và đây chính là phần khiến mọi người mất cảnh giác. Ở phần lớn các bang của Mỹ, tang lễ tại nhà là hoàn toàn hợp pháp. Chỉ một số tiểu bang yêu cầu giám đốc tang lễ được cấp phép phải tham gia vào quá trình chôn cất. Ở hầu hết đất nước, bạn có thể giữ thi thể ở nhà một cách hợp pháp, tắm rửa và tự mặc nó, đặt nó trong một tấm vải liệm hoặc một hộp gỗ đơn giản, và chôn nó trên đất tư miễn là bạn nộp đủ giấy tờ hợp lệ và tuân theo các quy định phân vùng của địa phương. Ngành tang lễ đã dành hơn một thế kỷ để tạo dựng ấn tượng rằng bạn cần họ. Về mặt pháp lý, ở hầu hết các nơi, bạn không làm như vậy. Phong trào chôn cất xanh đã phát triển cùng với điều này. Thi thể được bọc trong tấm vải cotton hoặc vải lanh đi thẳng vào lòng đất với tốc độ độ sâu cho phép sự phân hủy tự nhiên thực hiện những gì nó luôn làm.
